9.t: Working with data: a monohybrid cross
q: Calculate the ratio of yellow to green for pod 2 and for Mendel’s total.
Deduce which allele is dominant and the genotype of the parent plant. Explain.
Yellow is dominant: the parent is yellow and produces about 3 yellow : 1 green, which only a heterozygote (Yy) selfed can give.
Calculate the expected numbers of yellow and green seeds on the whole plant.
Explain why single pods differ so much from 3 : 1 but Mendel’s total is very close.
Fertilisation is random: small samples show large chance deviations; in a very large sample these average out.
Outline how you could find out whether a yellow seed from this plant is YY or Yy.
Test cross the plant grown from it with a green (yy) plant: all yellow offspring means YY; about half green means Yy.

26.t: Working with data: comparing two groups
q: Calculate the interquartile range of class 1 and class 2.
Class 1: 20 − 18 = 2 cm. Class 2: 21 − 17 = 4 cm.
Show whether 28 cm is an outlier in class 2. (Outlier: more than 1.5 × IQR above Q3.)
Q3 + 1.5 × 4 = 21 + 6 = 27 cm. 28 is above 27, so it is an outlier.
Compare the distributions of hand span in classes 1 and 2.
The medians are similar (19 and 18 cm), but class 2 is more spread out (IQR 4 against 2; range 8 against 6).
Hand span shows continuous variation. Explain its two causes.
It is polygenic (many genes, each adding a little) and affected by the environment (nutrition, growth).
A student says class 3 has smaller hands because of their genes. Evaluate this claim.
Age is a confounding variable: 12-year-olds are still growing. We cannot separate genes from age here; we would need to compare people of the same age.
